hero.title: Why objects?
intro.0: Why bother with classes and methods at all - why not put everything in one big Main? It seems simpler at first. But as a program grows, loose data and scattered rules get hard to keep straight. Here you'll see what objects give you: data and the rules around it, kept in one place you can trust.
task.1.title: Write a class to hold state
task.1.context: Loose variables drift apart - it is easy to print one cat's name next to another cat's mischief. A `class` ties related data into one thing. Write a `Cat` class that holds a `Name` and whether it `KnockedSomethingOver`, so they always travel together.
task.1.goal.0: Write a `Cat` class with a `Name` (string) and a `KnockedSomethingOver` (bool).
task.1.goal.1: Main builds Mittens (guilty) and prints the result, so the output is Mittens: True.
task.2.title: Put the behaviour with the data
task.2.context: An object keeps the behaviour beside the state it needs. The `Cat` already holds its data; now give it a `Verdict()` method that turns that data into a sentence. Write the method so the cat that knows what it did also knows how to own up to it.
task.2.goal.0: Add a `Verdict()` method to `Cat`. It returns the `Name`, then `": guilty"` if it knocked something over, otherwise `": innocent"`.
task.2.goal.1: Main judges Mittens (guilty), so the output is Mittens: guilty.
task.3.title: Hide the inside
task.3.context: If a count is a public field, any line anywhere can set it to nonsense. Write a `ScoreBoard` class that keeps its count `private`, so only the class itself can change it. The outside adds to it through a method and reads it through another - it can never reach in and corrupt it.
task.3.goal.0: Write a `ScoreBoard` with a `private` count, a `Give(bool goodBoy)` that adds one only when `goodBoy` is true, and a `Total()` that returns the count.
task.3.goal.1: Main gives to true, true, false, so the output is 2.
task.4.title: Guard the rule
task.4.context: Hiding the field lets the class defend it. Write a `Bowl` whose food can never drop because of a silly amount: `Fill` adds scoops only when the number is positive, so a negative or zero is ignored. The bowl keeps itself sensible no matter who calls it.
task.4.goal.0: Write a `Bowl` with a `private` food count, a `Fill(int scoops)` that ignores amounts of 0 or less, and an `Amount()` that returns the food.
task.4.goal.1: Main fills 10, then -5 (ignored), then 3, so the output is 13.
task.5.title: Change it in one place
task.5.context: By now you hide state and reach it through methods. A cat has nine lives. Write a `Cat` that is told how many lives are `used` in its constructor, keeps that count in a `private` field, and offers a `LivesLeft()` that returns `9 - used`. Main makes a couple of cats and asks each how many lives are left - the nine-lives rule lives in one private place.
task.5.goal.0: Write a `Cat` whose constructor takes how many lives are `used`, stored in a `private` field, with a `LivesLeft()` returning `9 - used`.
task.5.goal.1: Main makes cats with 1 and 3 lives used, so the output is two lines: 8 then 6.
task.6.title: Why objects? - recap
task.6.context: That is why we bother with classes and methods instead of one long Main.
task.6.summaryIntro: Objects exist so related data and the rules that guard it live together, instead of being scattered through one giant Main.
task.6.summaryItems.0.title: Group state -
task.6.summaryItems.0.text: a `class` keeps related data together as one thing.
task.6.summaryItems.1.title: Behaviour with state -
task.6.summaryItems.1.text: put a method next to the data it works on.
task.6.summaryItems.2.title: private -
task.6.summaryItems.2.text: hide a field so only the class can change it.
task.6.summaryItems.3.title: Guard the rule -
task.6.summaryItems.3.text: the one method that writes can reject nonsense.
task.6.summaryItems.4.title: One reason to change -
task.6.summaryItems.4.text: fix a rule once inside the object and every caller follows.
